stimulus.body: A short reference note on testing a warrant is set for a close-reading task. It states: Jokes often have target-language equivalents. A marginal reminder adds: test the warrant first. Four statements are then offered, and only one of them follows from what the note actually says.

questions.stem: This item turns on “Evaluate whether a warrant supports the claim / Test the warrant first. / Testing a warrant”. Which of the four options is warranted?

answer.exemplar: The warrant that jokes are untranslatable is false; jokes can be adapted with equivalents, so the note should test the warrant before keeping the source joke.

questions.explanation: The passage gives the controlling distinction: jokes often have target-language equivalents. On that basis "The warrant that jokes are untranslatable is false; jokes can be adapted with equivalents, so…" is the supported choice.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Recognize a forced choice ignoring alternatives

stimulus.body: Note TR-453 claims a register must be either elevated or colloquial, ignoring standard register. register is not limited to elevated or colloquial. A marginal reminder adds: look for middle options. Four statements are offered, and only one follows from the note.

questions.stem: A reviewer is weighing competing claims about false dilemma, among them "Standard register never occurs". Based only on the excerpt above, which answer is the one the evidence warrants?

options.text: Elevated and colloquial are the only registers.
It forces a binary while ignoring standard register.

options.misconception: substitutes a familiar but inapplicable case for the relation the passage establishes

questions.explanation: What settles the item is the relation stated in the passage: what settles the item is the relation stated in the passage: register is not limited to elevated or colloquial. On that basis "It forces a binary while ignoring standard register" is the supported choice. Option A ("Standard register never occurs") fails because it dismisses middle option; Option B ("Elevated and colloquial are the only registers") fails because it accepts false binary; Option D ("All registers are elevated") fails because it substitutes a familiar but inapplicable case for false dilemma.

questions.stem: The cue supplied for this item is “Recognize authority cited beyond its expertise / Match authority to field. / Authority outside its field”. Which option follows from it?

options.text: An athlete lacks authority in grammar.

questions.learningObjective: Check whether premises support the conclusion

stimulus.body: The working note below records the evidence for a claim about validity and premise structure. the conclusion follows from the premises, so the argument is valid despite a false premise. A marginal reminder adds: validity concerns form. A reader must decide which of the four proposed statements the note warrants, without using outside knowledge.

questions.stem: The controlling cue here is “Check whether premises support the conclusion / Validity concerns form. / Validity and premise structure”. Which option is consistent with it?

options.text: A false premise makes the conclusion false though form is valid.

options.misconception: selects "No primes are odd" where the rule in the passage requires a different condition

questions.explanation: What settles the item is the relation stated in the passage: the conclusion follows from the premises, so the argument is valid despite a false premise. On that basis "A false premise makes the conclusion false though form is valid" is the supported choice. Option A ("2 is not prime") fails because it adds false taxonomy; Option B ("The argument is invalid") fails because it confuses false premise with invalidity; Option D ("No primes are odd") fails because it selects "No primes are odd" where validity and premise structure requires a different condition.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Spot a word shifting meaning mid-argument

stimulus.body: Note TR-458 argues a sentence is bright because it has light, then calls it bright in mood. the argument trades on two senses of bright. A marginal reminder adds: track the word's senses. Four statements are offered, and only one follows from the note.

questions.stem: A reader keeps “Spot a word shifting meaning mid-argument / Track the word's senses. / Equivocation” in mind while checking the excerpt. Which choice follows?

options.misconception: selects "Bright always means light" where the rule in the passage requires a different condition
treats "Mood is always bright" as if it followed from the evidence

options.text: The word bright shifts from light to mood.

questions.explanation: The passage gives the controlling distinction: the passage gives the controlling distinction: the argument trades on two senses of bright. On that basis "The word bright shifts from light to mood" is the supported choice. Option A ("Light never matters") fails because it dismisses light sense; Option B ("Bright always means light") fails because it selects "Bright always means light" where equivocation requires a different condition; Option C ("Mood is always bright") fails because it treats "Mood is always bright" as if it followed from the evidence.

options.text: Shortness of source does not imply expansion is needed.

options.misconception: mistakes a surface feature of "Long texts never need expansion" for the governing rule

On that basis "Shortness of source does not imply expansion is needed" is the supported choice. Option A ("Short texts always need expansion") fails because it treats shortness as expansion proof; Option C ("Expansion is always good") fails because it adds value judgment; Option D ("Long texts never need expansion") fails because it mistakes a surface feature of "Long texts never need expansion" for the governing rule.
